body.text: The first thing that catches the eye is the Amar Kanth, a towering canvas that tells the origin story of the River Narmada. Figures and details fill its surface, drawing the eye from one scene to another. The canvas is tall enough to reach the first-floor balcony of DakshinaChitra Heritage Museum in Chennai, where the exhibition “Myth, Memory, Form” is on view. In its foreground, Achyut Siddu and Apoorva Mishra, founders of Loksutr, an organisation that works with oral and intangible knowledge, inaugurated the exhibition.

Open to the public until the first weekend of December, the exhibition asks its audience to look at the stories and processes behind the works on display. Before the paintings were paintings, they were myths and memories. Some came from centuries-old texts; others are stories passed down within the Gond community of Madhya Pradesh, one of the largest tribes in India. Loksutr has collaborated with 10 artists to give these stories visual form: 21 Patachitra frames, 24 Gond frames, and one large canvas.

Gond’s art history, in the form we see today, is far shorter than the stories it depicts. Its modern form can be traced to a single artist: Jangarh Singh Shyam of Patangarh, Madhya Pradesh. J. Swaminathan, founding director of Bharat Bhavan, a cultural centre in Bhopal, sent teams across the State in search of visual arts. One such team came across the teenage Jangarh, whose paintings covered the walls of his home. In Bhopal, he began to paint his lineage on canvas, and eventually, his family and community joined him. That lineage runs through every Gond work in the exhibition.

A 7.5-metre-long scroll titled The Pradhaan Continuum tells the story of the Gond artists themselves. Within the Gond tribe, Pradhaans form a smaller sub-community with an important role. Speaking to Frontline, Siddu explains, “Many communities in India have dedicated people who maintain oral records of their lineage. The Pradhaans play that role within the Gond tribe.” Every three years, a Pradhaan performs this ritual at their patron’s house, re-narrating their lineage and traditional songs on a three-stringed instrument called the bana. Referring to the accordion scroll, he adds, “And this book talks about how they became those genealogists. It’s the story behind how it all began.”

The process of creating the scroll was a revealing one for young Gond artist Ajay Marko. “I was young, and it was the first time I got an offer. I couldn’t say no,” he recalls. His interest in painting began when he was much younger, and he learnt the craft from his older brother. Working on the scroll led him to appreciate what his work meant and its place in society. “I didn’t have that much knowledge about the Pradhaan community, what all we do,” he says. “When I was working on the book, I understood it more.” Eighteen when the collaboration began, Marko found himself discovering a tradition he had inherited but not fully understood. His earlier work originated from an interest in painting; now, he sees himself as part of a community he can protect and represent.

Amar Kanth, created by four Gond artists, Brajbhushan Dhurve, Kaushal Prasad Tekam, Mithilesh Shyam, and Virendra Dhurve, is a familiar form of storytelling for anyone acquainted with Gond art: a long narrative in a single frame. Figures and details fill the canvas, pulling viewers closer. The tale it depicts is well known too. Lord Siva is immortal, but Goddess Parvati is not. When she questions him about it, his explanation leads to the birth of Narmada. This origin story is popular in the Gond region, where the river itself originates, and has been rendered several times. “What we have done differently is just sequentialising it,” Siddu explains.

This time, the scale is smaller, with 24 frames instead of one. In The Whispers of Immortality, artist Kailash Pradhaan breaks the story of Narmada into individual scenes. The story is the same, but the way it is read changes. As Siddu narrates each frame to the inaugural audience, the narrative unfolds across the gallery wall, with a beginning, middle, and end.
An old craft in new forms

“This is not how Gond painting is made,” Pradhaan says. “What we usually do was stuck in our heads, so we had to try harder to make something different. It took a lot of time, but it also felt good to make the story like that.” He has practised the craft for about 20 years and wants to safeguard the tradition while allowing it to change. Gond artists paint on paper and canvas; now their work also appears in books and on clothes. “Anything new we make, we still want our tradition to be a part of it,” Pradhaan says.

That instinct to carry tradition forward takes a different shape in the work of acclaimed Patachitra artist Prahallad Moharana. His challenge is to excavate a story from fragments of ancient texts. The 21 frames of Smriti Sūtradhāra, created by a team led by Moharana, depict the origin of painting, stitching together a narrative from fragments of different classical texts. The first chapter of the Chitralakshan, a long Sanskrit narrative that now survives in its Tibetan version, is attributed to King Nagnajit of Gandhara. It contains a legend about the origin of painting and was a major inspiration for Moharana’s work.

Moharana has been painting for 38 years and received the Kalidas Samman in 2006 and the President’s Award in 2025. He has worked extensively on stories from the Kumarasambhava, the Skanda Purana and the Vishnu Purana, among other texts. What he found different about Smriti Sūtradhāra was that its story had never been painted before. “Nobody has done this story before,” Moharana says. “Pehla number main hi hoon [I am the first].” He believes painting to be a god-given gift, which made the process of reconstructing its origin particularly important to him. “It [painting] came from above. So how did it come? Who brought it? All these things are within the story. I’ve searched for all the little things.”

Siddu says, “You will see that what we have presented doesn’t exist as a single narrative.” The paintings are the last step in the process. Siddu describes the process as “co-creative”, with the works emerging from collaboration between the artists and Loksutr.

The starting point was where each story began: an oral narration by the artists themselves. From there, the team sat together to identify what Siddu calls “event nodes”, moments in the story with the greatest potential to be visualised. This was followed by storyboarding, with rough pencil sketches laid out on the ground, compared, and reworked until a sequence took shape. Only then did colour enter the process, mixed scene by scene with Mishra before the artists began painting.

The most challenging part was finding imagery that could translate beyond the community. A gesture that means something in one cultural context may mean little outside it. In trying to find a visual metaphor for doubt, Siddu explains, “It might indicate doubt in some parts of India, but maybe people don’t express doubt like that elsewhere.”

Patachitra is a centuries-old art form, while Gond painting in its modern form is relatively new. The two sit side by side at “Myth, Memory, Form”, bringing together different traditions of storytelling. The exhibition also shows how stories change when they move between forms: from ancient text to Patachitra, or from a single frame to 24. “There is some sensitivity that opens up within the people, and they try themselves to uncover what meaning the narrative is trying to give,” says Siddu, hoping that visitors take away something beyond the image.
Diya Mantha is an intern at Frontline from July till October, 2026.
